entries.30d8e5f917adbdc79e102b50c376c49a29ccb5ee: <div sID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Judg.4" sID="Judg.4"/> <div eID="gen4661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4662" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen4663" type="x-p"/> The method of the history of Deborah and Barak (the heroes in this chapter) is the same with that before. Here is, I. Israel revolted from God, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Israel oppressed by Jabin, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.2-Judg.4.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. Israel judged by Deborah, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.4-Judg.4.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. IV. Israel rescued out of the hands of Jabin. 1. Their deliverance is concerted between Deborah and Barak, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.6">ver. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.9">9</reference>. 2. It is accomplished by their joint-agency. Barak takes the field, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.10">ver. 10</reference>. Sisera, Jabin's general, meets him, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.12-Judg.4.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. Deborah encourages him, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.14">ver. 14</reference>. And God gives him a complete victory. The army routed, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.15-Judg.4.16">ver. 15, 16</reference>. The general forced to flee, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">ver. 17</reference>. And where he expected shelter he had his life stolen from him by Jael while he was asleep (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.18-Judg.4.21">ver. 18-21</reference>), which completes Barak's triumph (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.22">ver. 22</reference>) and Israel's deliverance, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.23-Judg.4.24">ver. 23, 24</reference>.
entries.6339f59a4bcf4d29f50fe13c2ca71f197c795ada: <div eID="gen4663" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen4662" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Israelites Enslaved by Jabin. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1285.)</title> <div sID="gen4664" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , when Ehud was dead. <hi type="super">2</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host <hi type="italic">was</hi> Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles. <hi type="super">3</hi> And the children of Israel cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : for he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel. <div eID="gen4664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4665" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Israel backsliding from God: They again <hi type="italic">did evil in his sight,</hi> forsook his service, and worshipped idols; for this was the sin which now most easily beset them, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.1">v. 1</reference>. See in this, 1. The strange strength of corruption, which hurries men into sin notwithstanding the most frequent experience of its fatal consequences. The bent to backslide is with great difficulty restrained. 2. The common ill effects of a long peace. The land had rest eighty years, which should have confirmed them in their religion; but, on the contrary, it made them secure and wanton, and indulgent of those lusts which the worship of the false gods was calculated for the gratification of. Thus <hi type="italic">the prosperity of fools destroys them. Jeshurun waxeth fat and kicketh.</hi> 3. The great loss which a people sustains by the death of good governors. <hi type="italic">The did evil, because Ehud was dead.</hi> So it may be read. He kept a strict eye upon them, restrained and punished every thing that looked towards idolatry, and kept them close to God's service. But, when he was gone, they revolted, fearing him more than God. <div eID="gen4665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4666" type="x-p"/> II. Israel oppressed by their enemies. When they forsook God, he forsook them; and then they became an easy prey to every spoiler. They alienated themselves from God as if he were none of theirs; and then God alienated them as none of his. Those that threw themselves out of God's service threw themselves out of his protection. <hi type="italic">What has my beloved to do in my house</hi> when she has thus played the harlot? <reference osisRef="Jer.11.15">Jer. xi. 15</reference>. He <hi type="italic">sold them into the hand of Jabin,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.4.2">v. 2</reference>. This Jabin reigned in Hazor, as another of the same name, and perhaps his ancestor, had done before him, whom Joshua routed and slew, and burnt his city, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Josh. xi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">10</reference>. But it seems, in process of time, the city was rebuilt, the power regained, the loss retrieved, and, by degrees, the king of Hazor becomes able to tyrannize over Israel, who by sin had lost all their advantage against the Canaanites. This servitude was longer than either of the former, and much more grievous. Jabin, and his general Sisera, did mightily oppress Israel. That which aggravated the oppression was, 1. That this enemy was nearer to them than any of the former, in their borders, in their bowels, and by this means had the more opportunity to do them a mischief. 2. That they were the natives of the country, who bore an implacable enmity to them, for invading and dispossessing them, and when they had them in their power would be so much the more cruel and mischievous towards them in revenge of the old quarrel. 3. That these Canaanites had formerly been conquered and subdued by Israel, were of old sentenced to be their servants (<reference osisRef="Gen.9.25">Gen. ix. 25</reference>), and might now have been under their feet, and utterly incapable of giving them any disturbance, if their own slothfulness, cowardice, and unbelief, had not suffered them thus to get head. To be oppressed by those whom their fathers had conquered, and whom they themselves had foolishly spared, could not but be very grievous. <div eID="gen4666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4667" type="x-p"/> III. Israel returning to their God: They <hi type="italic">cried unto the Lord,</hi> when distress drove them to him, and they saw no other way of relief. Those that slight God in their prosperity will find themselves under a necessity of seeking him when they are in trouble.
entries.9fb4a7a6e2eca50dbb333d58cfc322606a346f95: <div eID="gen4667" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Project of Deborah and Barak. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1258.)</title> <div sID="gen4668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time. <hi type="super">5</hi> And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Beth-el in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment. <hi type="super">6</hi> And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedesh-naphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel commanded, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun? <hi type="super">7</hi> And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand. <hi type="super">8</hi> And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, <hi type="italic">then</hi> I will not go. <hi type="super">9</hi> And she said, I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. And Deborah arose, and went with Barak to Kedesh. <div eID="gen4668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4669" type="x-p"/> The year of the redeemed at length came, when Israel was to be delivered out of the hands of Jabin, and restored again to their liberty, which we may suppose the northern tribes, that lay nearest to the oppressors and felt most the effects of his fury, did in a particular manner cry to God for. <hi type="italic">For the oppression of the poor, and the sighing of the needy, now will</hi> God <hi type="italic">arise.</hi> Now here we have, <div eID="gen4669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4670" type="x-p"/> I. The preparation of the people for their deliverance, by the prophetic conduct and government of Deborah, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.4-Judg.4.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Her name signifies a <hi type="italic">bee;</hi> and she answered her name by her industry, sagacity, and great usefulness to the public, her sweetness to her friends and sharpness to her enemies. She is said to be <hi type="italic">the wife of Lapidoth;</hi> but, the termination not being commonly found in the name of a man, some make this the name of a place: she was <hi type="italic">a woman of Lapidoth.</hi> Others take it appellatively, Lapidoth signifies <hi type="italic">lamps.</hi> The Rabbin say she had employed herself in making wicks for the lamps of the tabernacle; and, having stooped to that mean office for God, she was afterwards thus preferred. Or she was a woman of <hi type="italic">illuminations,</hi> or of <hi type="italic">splendours,</hi> one that was extraordinarily knowing and wise, and so came to be very eminent and illustrious. Concerning her we are here told, 1. That she was intimately acquainted with God; she was <hi type="italic">a prophetess,</hi> one that was instructed in divine knowledge by the immediate inspiration of the Spirit of God, and had gifts of wisdom, to which she attained not in an ordinary way: she <hi type="italic">heard the words of God,</hi> and probably <hi type="italic">saw the visions of the Almighty.</hi> 2. That she was entirely devoted to the service of Israel. She judged Israel at the time that Jabin oppressed them; and perhaps, being a woman, she was the more easily permitted by the oppressor to do it. She judged, not as a princess, by an civil authority conferred upon her, but as a prophetess, and as God's mouth to them, correcting abuses and redressing grievances, especially those which related to the worship of God. The children of Israel came up to her from all parts for judgment, not so much for the deciding of controversies between man and man as for advice in the reformation of what was amiss in things pertaining to God. Those among them who before had secretly lamented the impieties and idolatries of their neighbours, but knew not where to apply for the restraining of them, now made their complaints to Deborah, who, by the sword of the Spirit, showing them the judgment of God, reduced and reclaimed many, and excited and animated the magistrates in their respective districts to put the laws in execution. It is said she <hi type="italic">dwelt,</hi> or, as some read it, she <hi type="italic">sat</hi> under a palm-tree, called ever after from her <hi type="italic">the palm-tree of Deborah.</hi> Either she had her house under that tree, a mean habitation which would couch under a tree, or she had her judgment-seat in the open air, under the shadow of that tree, which was an emblem of the justice she sat there to administer, which will thrive and grow against opposition, as palms under pressures. Josephus says that the children of Israel came to Deborah, to desire her to pray to God for them, that they might be delivered out of the hand of Jabin; and Samuel is said at one particular time to judge Israel in Mizpeh, that is, to bring them back again to God, when they made the same address to him upon a like occasion, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.6">1 Sam. vii. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.7.8">8</reference>. <div eID="gen4670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4671" type="x-p"/> II. The project laid for their deliverance. When the children of Israel <hi type="italic">came to her for judgment,</hi> with her they found salvation. So those that seek to God for grace shall have grace and peace, grace and comfort, grace and glory. She was not herself fit to command an army in person, being a woman; but she nominated one that was fit, Barak of Naphtali, who, it is probable, had already signalized himself in some rencounters with the forces of the oppressor, living near him (for Hazor and Harosheth lay within the lot of that tribe), and thereby had gained a reputation and interest among his people. Some struggles, we may suppose, that brave man had made towards the shaking off of the yoke, but could not effect it till he had his commission and instructions from Deborah. He could do nothing without her head, nor she without his hands; but both together made a complete deliverer, and effected a complete deliverance. The greatest and best are not self-sufficient, but need one another. <div eID="gen4671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4672" type="x-p"/> 1. By God's direction, she orders Barak to raise an army, and engage Jabin's forces, that were under Sisera's command, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.6-Judg.4.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Barak, it may be, had been meditating some great attempt against the common enemy; a spark of generous fire was glowing in his breast, and he would fain do something to the purpose for his people and for the cities of his God. But two things discouraged him: <div eID="gen4672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4673" type="x-p"/> (1.) He wanted a commission to levy forces; this therefore Deborah here gives him under the broad seal of heaven, which, as a prophetess, she had a warrant to affix to it: "<hi type="italic">Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded it?</hi> Yet, certainly he has; take my word for it." Some think she intends this as an appeal to Barak's own heart. "Has not God, by a secret whisper to thyself, given thee some intimation of his purpose to make use of thee as an instrument in his hands to save Israel? Hast not thou felt some impulse of this kind upon thy own spirit?" If so, the spirit of prophesy in Deborah confirms the spirit of a soldier in Barak: <hi type="italic">Go and draw towards Mount Tabor.</hi> [1.] She directs him what number of men to raise-10,000; and let him not fear that these will be too few, when God hath said he will by them save Israel. [2.] Whence he should raise them—only out of his own tribe, and that of Zebulun next adjoining. These two counties should furnish him with an army sufficient; he need not stay to go further. And, [3.] She orders him where to make his rendezvous—at Mount Tabor, in his own neighbourhood. <div eID="gen4673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4674" type="x-p"/> (2.) When he had an army raised, he knew not how he should have an opportunity of engaging the enemy, who perhaps declined fighting, having heard that Israel, if they had but courage enough to make head against any enemy, seldom failed of success. "Well," says Deborah, in the name of "God, <hi type="italic">I will draw unto thee Sisera and his army.</hi>" She assured him that the matter should be determined by one pitched battle, and should not be long in the doing. [1.] In mentioning the power of the enemy, Sisera, a celebrated general, bold and experienced, his chariots, his iron chariots, and his multitude of soldiers, she obliged Barak to fortify himself with the utmost degree of resolution; for the enemy he was to engage was a very formidable one. It is good to know the worst, that we may provide accordingly. But, [2.] In fixing the very place to which Sisera would draw his army, she gave him a sign, which might help to confirm his faith when he came to engage. it was a contingent things, and depended upon Sisera's own will; but, when afterwards Barak should see the event falling out just as Deborah had foretold, he might thence infer that certainly in the rest she said she spoke under a divine direction, which would be a great encouragement to him, especially because with this, [3.] She gave him an express promise of success <hi type="italic">I will</hi> (that is, God will, in whose name I speak) <hi type="italic">deliver them into thy hand;</hi> so that when he saw them drawn up against him, according to Deborah's word, he might be confident that, according to her word, he should soon see them fallen before him. Observe, God <hi type="italic">drew them to him</hi> only that he might <hi type="italic">deliver them into his hand.</hi> When Sisera drew his forces together, he designed the destruction of Israel; but God <hi type="italic">gathered them as sheaves into the floor,</hi> for their own destruction, <reference osisRef="Mic.4.11-Mic.4.12">Mic. iv. 11, 12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Assemble yourselves, and you shall be broken to pieces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.8.9">Isa. viii. 9</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Rev.19.17-Rev.19.18">Rev. xix. 17, 18</reference>. <div eID="gen4674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4675" type="x-p"/> 2. At Barak's request, she promises to go along with him to the field of battle. (1.) Barak insisted much upon the necessity of her presence, which would be to him better than a council of war (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.8">v. 8</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If thou wilt go with me</hi> to direct and advise me, and in every difficult case to let me know God's mind, <hi type="italic">then I will go</hi> with all my heart, and not fear the chariots of iron; otherwise not." Some make this to be the language of a weak faith; he could not take her word unless he had her with him in pawn, as it were, for performance. It seems rather to arise from a conviction of the necessity of God's presence and continual direction, a pledge and earnest of which he would reckon Deborah's presence to be, and therefore begged thus earnestly for it. "<hi type="italic">If thou go not up with me,</hi> in token of God's going with me, <hi type="italic">carry me not up hence.</hi>" Nothing would be a greater satisfaction to him than to have the prophetess with him to animate the soldiers and to be consulted as an oracle upon all occasions. (2.) Deborah promised to go with him, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.9">v. 9</reference>. No toil nor peril shall discourage her from doing the utmost that becomes her to do for the service of her country. She would not send him where she would not go herself. Those that in God's name call others to their duty should be very ready to assist them in it. Deborah was the weaker vessel, yet had the stronger faith. But though she agrees to go with Barak, if he insists upon it, she gives him a hint proper enough to move a soldier not to insist upon it: <hi type="italic">The journey thou undertakest</hi> (so confident was she of the success that she called his engaging in war but the undertaking of a journey) <hi type="italic">shall not be for thy honour;</hi> not so much for thy honour as if thou hadst gone by thyself; for <hi type="italic">the Lord shall sell Sisera</hi> (now his turn comes to be sold as Israel was, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.2">v. 2</reference>, by way of reprisal) "<hi type="italic">into the hands of a woman;</hi>" that is, [1.] The world would ascribe the victory to the hand of Deborah: this he might himself foresee. [2.] God (to correct his weakness) would complete the victory by the hand of Jael, which would be some eclipse to his glory. But Barak values the satisfaction of his mind, and the good success of his enterprise, more than his honour; and therefore will by no means drop his request. He dares not fight unless he have Deborah with him, to direct him and pray for him. She therefore stood to her word with a masculine courage; this noble heroine <hi type="italic">arose and went with Barak.</hi>
entries.d00d73132c9298568339f160de22a113997f2204: <div eID="gen4675" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Defeat of Sisera. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1258.)</title> <div sID="gen4676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> And Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh; and he went up with ten thousand men at his feet: and Deborah went up with him. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now Heber the Kenite, <hi type="italic">which was</hi> of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> by Kedesh. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they showed Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam was gone up to mount Tabor. <hi type="super">13</hi> And Sisera gathered together all his chariots, <hi type="italic">even</hi> nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people that <hi type="italic">were</hi> with him, from Harosheth of the Gentiles unto the river of Kishon. <hi type="super">14</hi> And Deborah said unto Barak, Up; for this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the day in which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gone out before thee? So Barak went down from mount Tabor, and ten thousand men after him. <hi type="super">15</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> discomfited Sisera, and all <hi type="italic">his</hi> chariots, and all <hi type="italic">his</hi> host, with the edge of the sword before Barak; so that Sisera lighted down off <hi type="italic">his</hi> chariot, and fled away on his feet. <hi type="super">16</hi> But Barak pursued after the chariots, and after the host, unto Harosheth of the Gentiles: and all the host of Sisera fell upon the edge of the sword; <hi type="italic">and</hi> there was not a man left. <div eID="gen4676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4677" type="x-p"/> Here, I. Barak beats up for volunteers, and soon has his quota of men ready, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Deborah had appointed him to raise an army of 10,000 men (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.6">v. 6</reference>), and so many he has presently <hi type="italic">at his feet,</hi> following him, and subject to his command. God is said to call us <hi type="italic">to his feet</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa. xli. 2</reference>), that is, into obedience to him. Some think it intimates that they were all footmen, and so the armies of the Jews generally were, which made the disproportion of strength between them and the enemy (who had horses and chariots) very great, and the victory the more illustrious; but the presence of God and his prophetess was abundantly sufficient to balance that disproportion. Barak had his men <hi type="italic">at his feet,</hi> which intimates their cheerfulness and readiness to attend him whithersoever he went, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. Though the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali were chiefly depended on, yet it appears by Deborah's song that some had come in to him from other tribes (Manasseh and Issachar), and more were expected that came not, from Reuben, Dan, and Asher, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.14-Judg.5.17">ch. v. 14-17</reference>. But these are overlooked here; and we are only told that to make his 10,000 men effective indeed <hi type="italic">Deborah went up with him.</hi> The <reference osisRef="Judg.4.11">11th verse</reference>, concerning the removal of Heber, one of the families of the Kenites, out of the wilderness of Judah, in the south, where those families had fixed themselves (<reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">ch. i. 16</reference>), into the northern country, comes in for the sake of what was to follow concerning the exploit of Jael, a wife of that family. <div eID="gen4677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4678" type="x-p"/> II. Sisera, upon notice of Barak's motions, takes the field with a very numerous and powerful army (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.12-Judg.4.13">v. 12, 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">They showed Sisera,</hi> that is, it was shown to him. Yet some think it refers to the Kenites, mentioned immediately before, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.11">v. 11</reference>. They gave Sisera notice of Barak's rendezvous, there being peace at this time between Jabin and that family, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">v. 17</reference>. Whether they intended it as a kindness to him or no, it served to accomplish what God had said by Deborah (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will draw unto thee Sisera.</hi> Sisera's confidence was chiefly in his chariots; therefore particular notice is taken of them, 900 <hi type="italic">chariots of iron,</hi> which, with the scythes fastened to their axle-trees, when they were driven into an army of footmen, did terrible execution. So ingenious have men been in inventing methods of destroying one another, to gratify those lusts <hi type="italic">from which come wars and fightings.</hi> <div eID="gen4678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4679" type="x-p"/> III. Deborah gives orders to engage the enemy, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.14">v. 14</reference>. Josephus says that when Barak saw Sisera's army drawn up, and attempting to surround the mountain on the top of which he and his forces lay encamped, his heart quite failed him, and he determined to retire to a place of greater safety; but Deborah animated him to make a descent upon Sisera, assuring him that this was the day marked out in the divine counsels for his defeat. "Now they appear most threatening they are ripe for ruin. The thing is as sure to be done as if it were done already: <hi type="italic">The Lord hath delivered Sisera into thy hand.</hi>" See how the work and honour of this great action are divided between Deborah and Barak; she, as the head, <hi type="italic">gives the word,</hi> he, as the hand, <hi type="italic">does the work.</hi> Thus does God dispense his gifts variously, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4-1Cor.12.11">1 Cor. xii. 4</reference>, &c. But, though ordinarily <hi type="italic">the head of the woman is the man</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.3">1 Cor. xi. 3</reference>), he that has the residue of the Spirit was pleased to cross hands, and to put the head upon the woman's shoulders, choosing the weak things of the world to shame the mighty, that no flesh might glory in his presence. It was well for Barak that he had Deborah with him; for she made up what was defective, 1. In his conduct, by telling him, <hi type="italic">This is the day.</hi> 2. In his courage, by assuring him of God's presence: "<hi type="italic">Has not the Lord gone out before thee?</hi> Darest not thou follow when thou hast God himself for thy leader?" Note, (1.) In every undertaking it is good to be satisfied that God goes before us, that we are in the way of our duty and under his direction. (2.) If we have ground to hope that God goes before us, we ought to go on with courage and cheerfulness. Be not dismayed at the difficulties thou meetest with in resisting Satan, in serving God, or suffering for him; for <hi type="italic">has not the Lord gone out before thee?</hi> Follow him fully then. <div eID="gen4679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4680" type="x-p"/> IV. God himself routs the enemy's army, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.15">v. 15</reference>. Barak, in obedience to Deborah's orders, went down into the valley, though there upon the plain the iron chariots would have so much the more advantage against him, quitting his fastnesses upon the mountain in dependence upon the divine power; for <hi type="italic">in vain is salvation hoped for from hills and mountains; in the Lord alone is the salvation of his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.3.23">Jer. iii. 23</reference>. And he was not deceived in his confidence: <hi type="italic">The Lord discomfited Sisera.</hi> It was not so much the bold and surprising alarm which Barak gave their camp that dispirited and dispersed them, but God's terror seized their spirits and put them into an unaccountable confusion. <hi type="italic">The stars,</hi> it seems, fought against them, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.20">ch. v. 20</reference>. Josephus says that a violent storm of hail which beat in their faces gave them this rout, disabled them, and drove them back; so that they became a very easy prey to the army of Israel, and Deborah's words were made good: "<hi type="italic">The Lord has delivered them into thy hand;</hi> it is now in thy power to do what thou wilt with them." <div eID="gen4680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4681" type="x-p"/> V. Barak bravely improves his advantage, follows the blow with undaunted resolution and unwearied diligence, prosecutes the victory, pursues the scattered forces, even to their general's head-quarters at Harosheth (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.16">v. 16</reference>), and spares none whom God had delivered into his hand to be destroyed: <hi type="italic">There was not a man left.</hi> When God goes before us in our spiritual conflicts we must bestir ourselves; and, when by grace he gives us some success against the enemies of our souls, we must improve it by watchfulness and resolution, and carry on the holy war with vigour.
entries.3d1d9f385c0eb50c7da40703741bdb42cfce22f5: <div eID="gen4681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Howbeit Sisera fled away on his feet to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite: for <hi type="italic">there was</hi> peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite. <hi type="super">18</hi> And Jael went out to meet Sisera, and said unto him, Turn in, my lord, turn in to me; fear not. And when he had turned in unto her into the tent, she covered him with a mantle. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he said unto her, Give me, I pray thee, a little water to drink; for I am thirsty. And she opened a bottle of milk, and gave him drink, and covered him. <hi type="super">20</hi> Again he said unto her, Stand in the door of the tent, and it shall be, when any man doth come and enquire of thee, and say, Is there any man here? that thou shalt say, No. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then Jael Heber's wife took a nail of the tent, and took an hammer in her hand, and went softly unto him, and smote the nail into his temples, and fastened it into the ground: for he was fast asleep and weary. So he died. <hi type="super">22</hi> And, behold, as Barak pursued Sisera, Jael came out to meet him, and said unto him, Come, and I will show thee the man whom thou seekest. And when he came into her <hi type="italic">tent,</hi> behold, Sisera lay dead, and the nail <hi type="italic">was</hi> in his temples. <hi type="super">23</hi> So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel. <hi type="super">24</hi> And the hand of the children of Israel prospered, and prevailed against Jabin the king of Canaan, until they had destroyed Jabin king of Canaan. <div eID="gen4682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4683" type="x-p"/> We have seen the army of the Canaanites totally routed. It is said (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.9-Ps.83.10">Ps. lxxxiii. 9, 10</reference>, where the defeat of this army is pleaded as a precedent for God's doing the like in after times) that they became <hi type="italic">as dung for the earth.</hi> Now here we have, <div eID="gen4683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4684" type="x-p"/> I. The fall of their general, Sisera, captain of the host, in whom, it is likely, Jabin their king put an entire confidence, and therefore was not himself present in the action. Let us trace the steps of this mighty man's fall. <div eID="gen4684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4685" type="x-p"/> 1. He quitted his chariot, and took to his feet, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.15">v. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">17</reference>. His chariots had been his pride and his confidence; and we may suppose he had therefore despised and defied the armies of the living God, because they were all on foot, and had neither chariot nor horse, as he had. Justly therefore is he thus made ashamed of his confidence, and forced to quit it, and thinks himself then most safe and easy when he has got clear of his chariot, though we may well suppose it the best made, and best drawn, of any of them. Thus are those disappointed who rest on the creature; like a broken reed, it not only breaks under them, but runs into their hand, and pierceth them with many sorrows. The idol may quickly become a burden (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa. xlvi. 1</reference>), and what we were sick for God can make us sick of. How miserable doth Sisera look now he is dismounted! It is hard to say whether he blusheth or trembleth more. Put not your trust in princes, if they may so soon be brought to this, if he who but lately trusted to his arms with so much assurance must now trust to his heels only with so little. <div eID="gen4685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4686" type="x-p"/> 2. He fled for shelter to the tents of the Kenites, having no strong-hold, nor any place of is own in reach to retire to. The mean and solitary way of the Kenites' living, perhaps, he had formerly despised and ridiculed, and the more because religion was kept up among them; yet now he is glad to put himself under the protection of one of these tents: and he chooses the wife's tent or apartment, either because less suspected, or because it happened to be next to him, and the first he came to, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.17">v. 17</reference>. And that which encouraged him to go thither was that at this time there was peace between his master and the house of Heber: not that there was any league offensive and defensive between them, only at present there were no indications of hostility. Jabin did them no harm, did not oppress them as he did the Israelites, their plain, quiet, harmless way of living making them not suspected nor feared, and perhaps God so ordering it as a recompence for their constant adherence to the true religion. Sisera thought he might therefore be safe among them; not considering that, though they themselves suffered not by Jabin's power, they heartily sympathized with the Israel of God that did. <div eID="gen4686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4687" type="x-p"/> 3. Jael invited him in, and bade him very welcome. Probably she stood at the tent door, to enquire what news from the army, and what the success of the battle which was fought not far off. (1.) She invited him in. Perhaps she stood waiting for an opportunity to show kindness to any distressed Israelite, if there should be occasion for it; but seeing Sisera come in great haste, panting and out of breath, she invited him to come and repose himself in her tent, in which, while she seemed to design the relieving of his fatigue, perhaps she really intended the retarding of his flight, that he might fall into the hands of Barak, who was not in a hot chase after him (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.18">v. 18</reference>), and it may well questioned whether she had at first any thought of taking away his life, but rather God afterwards put it into her heart. (2.) She made very much of him, and seemed mighty careful to have him easy, as her invited guest. Was he weary? she finds him a very convenient place to repose himself in, and recruit his strength. Was he thirsty? well he might. Did he want a little water to cool his tongue? the best liquor her tent afforded was at his service, and that was milk (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.19">v. 19</reference>), which, we may suppose, he drank heartily of, and, being refreshed with it, was the better disposed to sleep. Was he cold, or afraid of catching cold? or did he desire to be hid from the pursuers, if they should search that tent? she covered him with a mantle, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.18">v. 18</reference>. All expressions of care for his safety. Only when he desired her to tell a lie for him, and to say he was not there, she declined making any such promise, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.20">v. 20</reference>. We must not sin against God, no, not to oblige those we would show ourselves most observant of. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> We must suppose she kept her tent as quiet as she could, and free from noise, that he might sleep the sooner and the faster. And now was Sisera least safe when he was most secure. How uncertain and precarious is human life! and what assurance can we have of it, when it may so easily be betrayed by those with whom it is trusted, and those may prove its destroyers who we hoped would be its protectors! It is best making God our friend, for he will not deceive us. <div eID="gen4687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4688" type="x-p"/> 4. When he lay fast asleep she drove a long nail through his temples, so fastened his head to the ground, and killed him, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.21">v. 21</reference>. And, though this was enough to do the business, yet, to make sure work (if we translate it rightly, <reference osisRef="Judg.5.26">ch. v. 26</reference>), she cut off his head, and left it nailed there. Whether she designed this or no when she invited him into her tent does not appear; probably the thought was darted into her mind when she saw him lie so conveniently to receive such a fatal blow; and, doubtless, the thought brought with it evidence sufficient that it came not from Satan as a murderer and destroyer, but from God as a righteous judge and avenger, so much of brightness and heavenly light did she perceive in the inducements to it that offered themselves, the honour of God and the deliverance of Israel, and nothing of the blackness of malice, hatred, or personal revenge. (1.) It was a divine power that enabled her to do it, and inspired her with a more than manly courage. What if her hand should shake, and she should miss her blow? What if he should awake when she was attempting it? Or suppose some of his own attendants should follow him, and surprise her in the face, how dearly would she and all hers be made to pay for it? Yet, obtaining help of God, she did it effectually. (2.) It was a divine warrant that justified her in the doing of it; and therefore, since no such extraordinary commissions can now be pretended, it ought not in any case to be imitated. The laws of friendship and hospitality must be religiously observed, and we must abhor the thought of betraying any whom we have invited and encouraged to put a confidence in us. And, as to this act of Jael (like that of Ehud in the chapter before), we have reason to think she was conscious of such a divine impulse upon her spirit to do it as did abundantly satisfy herself (and it ought therefore to satisfy us) that it was well done. God's judgments are a great deep. The instrument of this execution was a nail of the tent, that is, one of the great pins with which the tent, or the stakes of it, were fastened. They often removing their tents, she had been used to drive these nails, and therefore knew how to do it the more dexterously on this great occasion. He that thought to destroy Israel with his many iron chariots is himself destroyed with one iron nail. Thus do the weak things of the world confound the mighty. See here Jael's glory and Sisera's shame. The great commander dies, [1.] In his sleep, fast asleep, and weary. It comes in as a reason why he stirred not, to make resistance. So fettered was he in the chains of sleep that he could not find his hands. Thus <hi type="italic">the stout-hearted are spoiled at thy rebuke, O God of Jacob! they are cast into a dead sleep,</hi> and so are made to sleep their last, <reference osisRef="Ps.76.5-Ps.76.6">Ps. lxxvi. 5, 6</reference>. Let not the strong man then glory in his strength; for when he sleeps where is it? It is weak, and he can do nothing; a child may insult him then, and steal his life from him; and yet if he sleep not he is soon spent and weary, and can do nothing either. Those words which we here put in a parenthesis (<hi type="italic">for he was weary</hi>) all the ancient versions read otherwise: <hi type="italic">he struggled</hi> (or started, as we say) <hi type="italic">and died,</hi> so the Syriac and Arabic, <hi type="italic">Exagitans sese mortuus est. He fainted and died,</hi> so the LXX. <hi type="italic">Consocians morte soporem,</hi> so the vulgar Latin, joining sleep and death together, seeing they are so near akin. <hi type="italic">He fainted and died.</hi> He dies, [2.] With his head nailed to the ground, an emblem of his earthly-mindedness. <hi type="italic">O curve in terram animæ!</hi> His ear (says bishop Hall) was fastened close to the earth, as if his body had been listening what had become of his soul. He dies, [3.] By the hand of a woman. This added to the shame of his death before men; and had he but known it, as Abimelech (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.54">ch. ix. 54</reference>), we may well imagine how much it would have added to the vexation of his own heart. <div eID="gen4688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4689" type="x-p"/> II. The glory and joy of Israel hereupon. 1. Barak their leader finds his enemy dead, (<reference osisRef="Judg.4.22">v. 22</reference>), and no doubt, he was very well pleased to find his work done so well to his hand, and so much to the glory of God and the confusion of his enemies. had he stood too nicely upon a point of honour, he would have resented it as an affront to have the general slain by any hand but his; but now he remembered that this diminution of his honour he was sentenced to undergo, for insisting upon Deborah's going with him (<hi type="italic">the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman</hi>), though then it was little thought that the prediction would be fulfilled in such a way as this. 2. Israel is completely delivered out of the hands of Jabin king of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Judg.4.23-Judg.4.24">v. 23, 24</reference>. They not only shook off his yoke by this day's victory, but they afterwards prosecuted the war against him, till they had destroyed him, he and his nation being by the divine appointment devoted to ruin and not to be spared. The Israelites, having soundly smarted for their foolish pity in not doing it before, resolved now it is in their power to indulge them no longer, but to make a thorough riddance of them, as a people to whom to show mercy was as contrary to their own interest as it was to God's command; and probably it is with an eye to the sentence they were under that this enemy is named three times here in these <reference osisRef="Judg.4.23-Judg.4.24">last two verses</reference>, and called <hi type="italic">king of Canaan;</hi> for as such he was to be destroyed; and so thoroughly was he destroyed that I do not remember to read of the kings of Canaan any more after this. The children of Israel would have prevented a great deal of mischief if they had sooner destroyed these Canaanites, as God had both commanded and enabled them; but better be wise late, and buy wisdom by experience, than never wise.  <chapter eID="Judg.4"/> <div eID="gen4689" type="x-p"/>

entries.eafb05e9e743e9247ec7e3caefe6cab3ec0c1b86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2233"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Judg.4.1-Judg.4.17">Jud 4:1-17</reference>. Deborah and Barak Deliver Israel from Jabin and Sisera.</title> <div sID="gen3011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2233"/><hi type="bold">1. The children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, when Ehud was dead--</hi>The removal of the zealous judge Ehud again left his infatuated countrymen without the restraint of religion. <div eID="gen3011" type="x-p"/>
entries.9e40f6b21aeada4d28406d4a736f448c9dddf847: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2234"/><div sID="gen3012" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2234"/><hi type="bold">2-3. Jabin king of Canaan--</hi>"Jabin," a royal title (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>). The second Jabin built a new capital on the ruins of the old (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.11">11</reference>). The northern Canaanites had recovered from the effect of their disastrous overthrow in the time of Joshua, and now triumphed in their turn over Israel. This was the severest oppression to which Israel had been subjected. But it fell heaviest on the tribes in the north, and it was not till after a grinding servitude of twenty years that they were awakened to view it as the punishment of their sins and to seek deliverance from God. <div eID="gen3012" type="x-p"/>
entries.09147ec4f96fba5ee5a1cbec362ce2165c7872e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2235"/><div sID="gen3013" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2235"/><hi type="bold">4. And Deborah, a prophetess--</hi>A woman of extraordinary knowledge, wisdom, and piety, instructed in divine knowledge by the Spirit and accustomed to interpret His will; who acquired an extensive influence, and was held in universal respect, insomuch that she became the animating spirit of the government and discharged all the special duties of a judge, except that of military leader.<div eID="gen3013" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the wife of Lapidoth--</hi>rendered by some, "a woman of splendors." <div eID="gen3014" type="x-p"/>
entries.9b0d0eb5f424ada8420d40dd6cc6f63d06a771ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2236"/><div sID="gen3015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2236"/><hi type="bold">5. she dwelt under the palm tree--</hi>or, collectively, "palm-grove." It is common still in the East to administer justice in the open air, or under the canopy of an umbrageous tree. <div eID="gen3015" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcaa510fa0bfb9c607b95ae43a84b14f87c0faa7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2237"/><div sID="gen3016" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2237"/><hi type="bold">6. she sent and called Barak--</hi>by virtue of her official authority as judge.<div eID="gen3016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kedesh-naphtali--</hi>situated on an eminence, little north of the Sea of Galilee, and so called to distinguish it from another Kedesh in Issachar.<div eID="gen3017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded?--</hi>a Hebrew form of making an emphatic communication.<div eID="gen3018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3019" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Go and draw toward mount Tabor--</hi>an isolated mountain of Galilee, northeast corner of the plain of Esdraelon. It was a convenient place of rendezvous, and the enlistment is not to be considered as limited to ten thousand, though a smaller force would have been inadequate. <div eID="gen3019" type="x-p"/>
entries.0a94d557febd6fb0c7eeac7e1834f14faa6b086c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2238"/><div sID="gen3020" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2238"/><hi type="bold">8. Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go--</hi>His somewhat singular request to be accompanied by Deborah was not altogether the result of weakness. The Orientals always take what is dearest to the battlefield along with them; they think it makes them fight better. The policy of Barak, then, to have the presence of the prophetess is perfectly intelligible as it would no less stimulate the valor of the troops, than sanction, in the eyes of Israel, the uprising against an oppressor so powerful as Jabin. <div eID="gen3020" type="x-p"/>
entries.844d0dbe06c9a2dbc1e9841810c03a9b6b4c2a1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2239"/><div sID="gen3021" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2239"/><hi type="bold">9. the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman--</hi>This was a prediction which Barak could not understand at the time; but the strain of it conveyed a rebuke of his unmanly fears. <div eID="gen3021" type="x-p"/>
entries.e91821acbfca124dc8983d29e9b00d0aace0055d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2240"/><div sID="gen3022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2240"/><hi type="bold">11. Now Heber the Kenite ... pitched his tent--</hi>It is not uncommon, even in the present day, for pastoral tribes to feed their flocks on the extensive commons that lie in the heart of inhabited countries in the East (see on <reference osisRef="Judg.1.16">Jud 1:16</reference>).<div eID="gen3022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3023" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">plain of Zaanaim--</hi>This is a mistranslation for "the oaks of the wanderers." The site of the encampment was under a grove of oaks, or terebinths, in the upland valley of Kedesh. <div eID="gen3023" type="x-p"/>
entries.8858a2afb4ad0b3d581bcd6371aed93133b168c6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2241"/><div sID="gen3024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2241"/><hi type="bold">13. the river of Kishon--</hi>The plain on its bank was chosen as the battlefield by Sisera himself, who was unconsciously drawn thither for the ruin of his army. <div eID="gen3024" type="x-p"/>
entries.e08d0edaf67059da8d94b277674c63530b2eae0b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2242"/><div sID="gen3025" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2242"/><hi type="bold">14. Barak went down from mount Tabor--</hi>It is a striking proof of the full confidence Barak and his troops reposed in Deborah's assurance of victory, that they relinquished their advantageous position on the hill and rushed into the plain in face of the iron chariots they so much dreaded. <div eID="gen3025" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b29033e64e3cdc539ed7803ebd50c7c85f3ccd8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2243"/><div sID="gen3026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2243"/><hi type="bold">15. the Lord discomfited Sisera--</hi>Hebrew, "threw his army into confusion"; men, horses, and chariots being intermingled in wild confusion. The disorder was produced by a supernatural panic (see on <reference osisRef="Judg.5.20">Jud 5:20</reference>).<div eID="gen3026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3027" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so that Sisera lighted down off his chariot, and fled away on his feet--</hi>His chariot being probably distinguished by its superior size and elegance, would betray the rank of its rider, and he saw therefore that his only chance of escape was on foot. <div eID="gen3027" type="x-p"/>
entries.b5a008ccd8353d577318e91bf8ffd907ef0fa41d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2244"/><div sID="gen3028" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2244"/><hi type="bold">16. But Barak pursued ... unto Harosheth--</hi>Broken and routed, the main body of Sisera's army fled northward; others were forced into the Kishon and drowned (see on <reference osisRef="Judg.5.21">Jud 5:21</reference>). <div eID="gen3028" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e44da1ffea780b804f73828c4f27e7600917b52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2245"/><div sID="gen3029" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2245"/><hi type="bold">17-18. Sisera fled ... to the tent of Jael--</hi>According to the usages of nomadic people, the duty of receiving the stranger in the sheik's absence devolves on his wife, and the moment the stranger is admitted into his tent, his claim to be defended or concealed from his pursuers is established. <div eID="gen3029" type="x-p"/>
entries.3deced673545c34d8e7ba2cb5ee180f21e3adf4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2246"/><div sID="gen3030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2246"/><hi type="bold">19. she ... gave him drink, and covered him--</hi>Sisera reckoned on this as a pledge of his safety, especially in the tent of a friendly sheik. This pledge was the strongest that could be sought or obtained, after he had partaken of refreshments, and been introduced in the inner or women's apartment. <div eID="gen3030" type="x-p"/>
entries.393e07747ce0a303d400aab301c9fcfc696c9ae7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2247"/><div sID="gen3031" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2247"/><hi type="bold">20. he said unto her, ... when any man doth come and enquire of thee and say, Is there any man here? that thou shalt say, No--</hi>The privacy of the harem, even in a tent, cannot be intruded on without express permission. <div eID="gen3031" type="x-p"/>
entries.b21e39657ff9f8f636a85030b445cebc68e5fa1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv2248"/><div sID="gen3032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv2248"/><hi type="bold">21. Then Jael took a nail of the tent--</hi>most probably one of the pins with which the tent ropes are fastened to the ground. Escape was almost impossible for Sisera. But the taking of his life by the hand of Jael was murder. It was a direct violation of all the notions of honor and friendship that are usually held sacred among pastoral people, and for which it is impossible to conceive a woman in Jael's circumstances to have had any motive, except that of gaining favor with the victors. Though predicted by Deborah [Jud 4:9], it was the result of divine foreknowledge only--not the divine appointment or sanction; and though it is praised in the song [Jud 5:24-27], the eulogy must be considered as pronounced not on the moral character of the woman and her deed, but on the public benefits which, in the overruling providence of God, would flow from it. <chapter eID="Judg.4"/>

entries.a65ebd3b902e5fc207e199c95d1fffefcd289cc8: <div eID="gen8456" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen8457" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8458" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8457" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> The Israelites again rebel against God, and they are delivered into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.1">Jdg 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.2">Jdg 4:2</reference>. They cry unto God, and he raises up Deborah and Barak to deliver then, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.3-Jdg.4.10">Jdg 4:3-10</reference>. Some account of Heber the Kenite, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.11">Jdg 4:11</reference>. Barak attacks Sisera, captain of Jabin's army, at the river Kishon, and gives him a total overthrow, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.12-Jdg.4.16">Jdg 4:12-16</reference>. Sisera leaves his chariot, and flies away on foot; enters the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber, by whom he is slain, while secreting himself in her apartment, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.17-Jdg.4.24">Jdg 4:17-24</reference>. <div eID="gen8459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen8460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> When Ehud was dead - Why not when Shamgar was dead? Does this not intimate that Shamgar was not reckoned in the number of the judges?
entries.d6655062b596851bf066be93ab29c812f0332c1d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen8461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> Jabin king of Canaan - Probably a descendant of the Jabin mentioned <reference osisRef="Jos.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>, etc., who had gathered together the wrecks of the army of that Jabin defeated by Joshua. Calmet supposes that these Canaanites had the dominion over the tribes of Naphtali, Zebulun, and Issachar; while Deborah judged in Ephraim, and Shamgar in Judah.
entries.9647463ae752994ec0fd2e177697f89eb7555208: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen8462" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> Nine hundred chariots of iron - Chariots armed with iron scythes, as is generally supposed; they could not have been made all of iron, but they might have been shod with iron, or had iron scythes projecting from the axle on each side, by which infantry might be easily cut down or thrown into confusion. The ancient Britons are said to have had such chariots.
entries.57d4c742881b2540584b6ef7e42ec30e15f593fa: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen8463" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> Deborah, a prophetess - One on whom the Spirit of God descended, and who was the instrument of conveying to the Israelites the knowledge of the Divine will, in things sacred and civil. <div eID="gen8464" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> She judged Israel - This is, I believe, the first instance of gynaecocrasy, or female government, on record. Deborah seems to have been supreme both in civil and religious affairs; and Lapidoth, her husband, appears to have had no hand in the government. But the original may as well be translated a woman of Lapidoth, as the wife of Lapidoth.
entries.298f8205820b3bd86e324bbf93d6e7d3423591b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen8465" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> The palm tree of Deborah - It is common for the Hindoos to plant trees in the names of themselves and their friends; and some religious mendicants live for a considerable time under trees. - Ward.
entries.d8ce37d38c69126f8d8c190aef004df9119677d7: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen8466" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> She sent and called Barak - She appointed him to be general of the armies on this occasion; which shows that she possessed the supreme power in the state. <div eID="gen8467" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8468" type="x-p"/> Mount Tabor - "Mount Tabor," says Maundrell, "stands by itself, about two or three furlongs within the plains of Esdraelon. It has a plain area at the top, both fertile and delicious of an oval figure, extending about one furlong in breadth, and two in length. The prospect from the top is beautiful: on the N.W. is the Mediterranean; and all around you have the spacious plains of Esdraelon and Galilee, which present you with a view of many places famous for the resort and miracles of the Son of God. At the bottom of Tabor, westward, stands Daberah, a small village, supposed to have taken its name from Deborah. Near this valley is the brook Kishon. During the rainy season, all the water that falls on the eastern side of the mountain, or upon the rising ground to the southward, empties itself into it, in a number of torrents: at which conjuncture it overflows its banks, acquires a wonderful rapidity, and carries all before it. It might be at such a time as this when the stars are said to fight against Sisera, <reference osisRef="Jdg.5.20">Jdg 5:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jdg.5.21">Jdg 5:21</reference>, by bringing an abundance of rain, whereby the Kishon became so high and rapid as to sweep away the host of Sisera, in attempting to ford it." See Maundrell and Shaw. This mountain is very difficult of ascent; it took Mr. Maundrell nearly an hour to reach the top; this, with its grand area on the summit, made a very proper place for the rendezvous of Barak's army. Antiochus used it for the same purpose in his wars; and Josephus appears to have fortified it; and Placidus, one of Vespasian's generals, was sent to reduce it. See more in Calmet.
entries.77b0f8cdd904bcd30386fe71d8245f3424afbc2e: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen8468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8469" type="x-p"/> The Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman - Does not this mean, If I go with thee, the conquest shall be attributed to me, and thou wilt have no honor? Or, is it a prediction of the exploit of Jael? In both these senses the words have been understood. It seems, however, more likely that Jael is intended. The Septuagint made a remarkable addition to the speech of Barak: "If thou wilt go with me I will go; but if thou wilt not go with me, I will not go; Ὁτι ουκ οιδα την ἡμεραν εν ῃ ευοδοι Κυριος τον αγγελον μετ' εμου, because I know not the day in which the Lord will send his angel to give me success." By which he appears to mean, that although he was certain of a Divine call to this work, yet, as he knew not the time in which it would be proper for him to make the attack, he wishes that Deborah, on whom the Divine Spirit constantly rested, would accompany him to let him know when to strike that blow, which he knew would be decisive. This was quite natural, and quite reasonable, and is no impeachment whatever of Barak's faith. St. Ambrose and St. Augustine have the same reading; but it is found in no MS. nor in any other of the versions. See <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.14">Jdg 4:14</reference>.
entries.96b1f28b78603980c6fa0bc4a9b04439789406b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen8469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8470" type="x-p"/> Ten thousand men at his feet - Ten thousand footmen. He had no chariots; his army was all composed of infantry.
entries.92d9f608fb80ba6fded27d46ade4e45a6d7b3e3d: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen8470" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8471" type="x-p"/> Hohab the father-in-law of Moses - For a circumstantial account of this person, and the meaning of the original word חתן chothen, which is translated son-in-law in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.14">Gen 19:14</reference>, see the notes on <reference osisRef="Exo.2.15">Exo 2:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.2.16">Exo 2:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.2.18">Exo 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.3.1">Exo 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.4.20">Exo 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.4.24">Exo 4:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.18.5">Exo 18:5</reference>.
entries.61e753a4378446d7e020785730c6f6356516d2a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen8471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8472" type="x-p"/> Up; for this is the day - This is exactly the purpose for which the Septuagint state, <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.8">Jdg 4:8</reference>, that Barak wished Deborah to accompany him. "I know not," says he, "The Day in which God will send his angel to give me prosperity: come thou with we that thou mayest direct me in this respect." She went, and told him the precise time in which he was to make the attack: Up, for This is the Day in which the Lord hath delivered Sisera into thine hand. <div eID="gen8472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8473" type="x-p"/> Went down from Mount Tabor - He had probably encamped his men on and near the summit of this mount. See the note on <reference osisRef="Jdg.4.6">Jdg 4:6</reference>.
entries.999a8fdaf61017b574c9d875fdc1fc1fabfadfdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen8473" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8474" type="x-p"/> The Lord discomfited Sisera - ויהם יהוה vayiahom Jehovah; the Lord Confounded, threw them all into confusion, drove them pell-mell - caused chariots to break and overthrow chariots, and threw universal disorder into all their ranks. In this case Barak and his men had little to do but kill and pursue, and Sisera in order to escape, was obliged to abandon his chariot. There is no doubt all this was done by supernatural agency; God sent his angel and confounded them.
entries.be65b7a1fd1d92b41a1dd68307070fb212e49f31: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen8474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8475" type="x-p"/> Jael went out to meet Sisera - He preferred the woman's tent because of secrecy; for, according to the etiquette of the eastern countries, no person ever intrudes into the apartments of the women. And in every dwelling the women have a separate apartment.
entries.2a1f786b27b0e68e8debaeb81228b2ed76b6e5ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen8475" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8476" type="x-p"/> She opened a bottle of milk - She gave more than he requested; and her friendship increased his confidence and security.
entries.501d4b4efa21718711624b390d87bfa239e501ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen8476" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8477" type="x-p"/> Stand in the door of the tent - As no man would intrude into the women's apartment without permission, her simply saying, there is no man in my tent, would preclude all search.
entries.c03a68f89ad2f8a565cf146b4f748ede18ccb10e: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen8477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8478" type="x-p"/> A nail of the tent - One of the spikes by which they fasten to the ground the cords which are attached to the cloth or covering. <div eID="gen8478" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8479" type="x-p"/> He was fast asleep and weary - As he lay on one side, and was overwhelmed with sleep through the heat and fatigues of the day, the piercing of his temples must have in a moment put him past resistance.
entries.76941a575fdaa9e630b57c06c661a524c932df46: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen8479" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8480" type="x-p"/> Behold, Sisera lay dead - What impression this made on the victorious Barak is not said: it could not give him much pleasure, especially when he learned the circumstances of his death.
entries.53e09b73b967369efed565589bdb910e97ef56f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen8480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> The hand of the children of Israel prospered - ותלך הלוך vattelech haloch, it went, going - they followed up this victory, and the consequence was, they utterly destroyed Jabin and his kingdom. It will naturally be expected that something should be said to justify the conduct of Jael: it must be owned that she slew Sisera in circumstances which caused the whole transaction to appear exceedingly questionable. They are the following: - <div eID="gen8481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8482" type="x-p"/> 1. There was peace between her family and the king of Canaan. <div eID="gen8482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> 2. That peace was no doubt made, as all transactions of the kind were, with a sacrifice and an oath. <div eID="gen8483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> 3. Sisera, knowing this, came to her tent with the utmost confidence. <div eID="gen8484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> 4. She met him with the most friendly greetings and assurances of safety. <div eID="gen8485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> 5. Having asked for water, to show her friendship and respect she gave him cream, and that in a vessel suitable to his dignity. <div eID="gen8486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> 6. She put him in the secret part of her own tent, and covered him in such a way as to evidence her good faith, and to inspire him with the greater confidence. <div eID="gen8487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> 7. She agreed to keep watch at the door, and deny his being there to any that might inquire. <div eID="gen8488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> 8. As she gave him permission to secrete himself with her, and gave him refreshment, she was bound by the rules of Asiatic hospitality to have defended his life, even at the risk of her own. <div eID="gen8489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> 9. Notwithstanding, she took the advantage of his weariness and deep sleep, and took away his life! <div eID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8491" type="x-p"/> 10. She exulted in her deed, met Barak, and showed him in triumph what she had done. <div eID="gen8491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8492" type="x-p"/> Now do we not find, in all this, bad faith, deceit, deep hypocrisy, lying, breach of treaty, contempt of religious rites, breach of the laws of hospitality, deliberate and unprovoked murder? But what can be said in her justification? All that can be said, and all that has been said is simply this: "She might have been sincere at first, but was afterwards Divinely directed to do what she did." If this was so, she is sufficiently vindicated by the fact; for God has a right to dispose of the lives of his creatures as he pleases: and probably the cup of Sisera's iniquity was full, and his life already forfeited to the justice of God. But does it appear that she received any such direction from God? There is no sufficient evidence of it: it is true that Deborah, a prophetess, declares her blessed above women; and this seems to intimate that her conduct was pleasing to God. If Deborah was inspired on this occasion, her words are a presumptive proof that the act was right; unless we are to understand it as a simple declaration of the reputation she should be held in among her own sex. But we do not find one word from Jael herself, stating how she was led to do an act repugnant to her feelings as a woman, contrary to good faith, and a breach of the rules of hospitality. Nor does the sacred penman say one word to explain the case; as in the case of Ehud, he states the fact, and leaves his readers to form their own opinion. To say, as has been said in the case of Eglon, that "Sisera was a public enemy, and any of the people whom he oppressed might be justified in taking away his life," is a very dangerous position, as it refers one of the most solemn acts of judgment and justice to the caprice, or prejudice, or enthusiastic feeling of every individual who may persuade himself that he is not only concerned in the business, but authorized by God to take vengeance by his own hand. While justice and law are in the world, God never will, as he never did, abandon cases of this kind to the caprice, prejudice, or party feeling, of any man. The conduct of Ehud and Jael are before the tribunal of God: I will not justify, I dare not absolutely condemn; there I leave them, and entreat my readers to do the like; after referring them to the observations at the end of the preceding chapter, where the subject is considered more at large.  <chapter eID="Judg.4"/> <div eID="gen8492" type="x-p"/>

entries.52e7ace74de3a941961117e5286e211cbe5aae41: <hi type="italic">The Victory over Jabin and His General Sisera</hi>. - Jdg 4:1-3. As the Israelites fell away from the Lord again when Ehud was dead, the Lord gave them into the hand of the Canaanitish king <hi type="italic">Jabin</hi>, who oppressed them severely for twenty years with a powerful army under <hi type="italic">Sisera</hi> his general. The circumstantial clause, “when Ehud was dead,” places the falling away of the Israelites from God in direct causal connection with the death of Ehud on the one hand, and the deliverance of Israel into the power of Jabin on the other, and clearly indicates that as long as Ehud lived he kept the people from idolatry (cf. Jdg 2:18-19), and defended Israel from hostile oppressions. Joshua had already conquered one king, <hi type="italic">Jabin</hi> of <hi type="italic">Hazor</hi>, and taken his capital (<reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.11.10">Jos 11:10</reference>). The king referred to here, who lived more than a century later, bore the same name. The name <hi type="italic">Jabin</hi>, “the discerning,” may possibly have been a standing name or title of the Canaanitish kings of Hazor, as Abimelech was of the kings of the Philistines (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.26.8">Gen 26:8</reference>). He is called “king of Canaan,” in distinction from the kings of other nations and lands, such as Moab, Mesopotamia, etc. (Jdg 3:8, Jdg 3:12), into whose power the Lord had given up His sinful people. <hi type="italic">Hazor</hi>, once the capital of the kingdoms of northern Canaan, was situated over (above or to the north of) Lake Huleh, in the tribe of Naphtali, but has not yet been discovered (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.11.1">Jos 11:1</reference>). Sisera, the general of Jabin, dwelt in <hi type="italic">Harosheth</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Goyim</hi>, and oppressed the Israelites most tyrannically (<hi type="italic">Mightily</hi>: cf. Jdg 7:1; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.16">1Sa 2:16</reference>) for twenty years with a force consisting of 900 chariots of iron (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.16">Jos 17:16</reference>). The situation of <hi type="italic">Harosheth</hi>, which only occurs here (Jdg 4:2, Jdg 4:13, Jdg 4:16), is unknown; but it is certainly to be sought for in one of the larger plains of Galilee, possibly the plain of <hi type="italic">Buttauf</hi>, where Sisera was able to develop his forces, whose strength consisted chiefly in war-chariots, and to tyrannize over the land of Israel.
entries.b9e1f22f0049ec38ae28941acb6945a20646e91e: Jdg 4:4-5 <div eID="gen3127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3128" type="x-p"/> At that time the Israelites were judged by <hi type="italic">Deborah</hi>, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who dwelt under the Deborah-palm between Ramah (er Râm: see at <reference osisRef="Josh.18.25">Jos 18:25</reference>) and Bethel (Beitin: see at <reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>) in the tribe of Benjamin, upon the mountains of Ephraim. Deborah is called נמיאה אשּׁה on account of her prophetic gift, like Miriam in <reference osisRef="Exod.15.20">Exo 15:20</reference>, and Hulda the wife of Shallum in 2Ki 22:14. This gift qualified her to judge the nation (the participle שׁפטה expresses the permanence of the act of judging), i.e., first of all to settle such disputes among the people themselves as the lower courts were unable to decide, and which ought therefore, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.17.8">Deu 17:8</reference>, to be referred to the supreme judge of the whole nation. The palm where she sat in judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>) was called after her the <hi type="italic">Deborah</hi>-palm. The Israelites went up to her there to obtain justice. The expression “<hi type="italic">came up</hi>” is applied here, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.8">Deu 17:8</reference>, to the place of justice, as a spiritual height, independently of the fact that the place referred to here really stood upon an eminence.
entries.3e444628c0a5b4711f6123058889d741ea0fb65e: Jdg 4:6-7 <div eID="gen3128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3129" type="x-p"/> But in order to secure the rights of her people against their outward foes also, she summoned <hi type="italic">Barak</hi> the son of Abinoam from Kedesh, in the tribe of Naphtali, on the west of the Huleh lake (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.12.22">Jos 12:22</reference>), and made known to him the commands of the Lord: “<hi type="italic">Up and draw to Mount Tabor, and take with thee 10,000 men of the children of Naphtali and Zebulun; and I will draw to thee into the brook-valley of Kishon, Sisera the captain of Jabin’s army, and his chariots, and his multitude</hi> (his men of war<hi type="italic">), and give him into thy hand.</hi>” משׁכתּ has been explained in different ways. <hi type="italic">Seb</hi>. <hi type="italic">Schmidt</hi>, <hi type="italic">Clericus</hi>, and others supply הקּרן or השּׁופר, draw with the trumpet (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.19.13">Exo 19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.6.5">Jos 6:5</reference>), i.e., blow the trumpet in long-drawn tones, upon Mount Tabor, and regard this as the signal for convening people; whilst <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi> (Diss. ii. pp. 76, 77) refers to Num 10:9, and understands the blowing of the horn as the signal by which the congregation of the Lord made known its need to Him, and appealed to Him to come to its help. It cannot indeed be proved that the blowing of the trumpet was merely the means adopted for convening the people together; in fact, the use of the following משׁכתּי, in the sense of draw, is to be explained on the supposition that משׁכתּ is used in a double sense. “The long-drawn notes were to draw the Lord to them, and then the Lord would draw to them Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army. Barak first calls the helper from heaven, and then the Lord calls the enemy upon earth.” Nevertheless we cannot subscribe to this explanation, <hi type="italic">first</hi> of all because the supposed ellipsis cannot be sustained in this connection, when nothing is said about the blowing of a trumpet either in what precedes or in what follows; and <hi type="italic">secondly</hi>, because Num 10:9 cannot be appealed to in explanation, for the simple reason that it treats of the blowing of the <hi type="italic">silver trumpets</hi> on the part of the priests, and they must not be confounded with the <hi type="italic">shopharoth</hi>. And the use made of the trumpets at Jericho cannot be transferred to the passage before us without some further ground. We are disposed therefore to take the word משׁך in the sense of <hi type="italic">draw</hi> (intransitive), i.e., proceed one after another in a long-drawn train (as in Jdg 20:37 and <reference osisRef="Exod.12.21">Exo 12:21</reference>), referring to the captain and the warriors drawing after him; whilst in Jdg 4:7 it is to be translated in the same way, though with a transitive signification. Mount Tabor, called Ἰταβύριον by the Greeks (see lxx Hos 5:1), the mountain of Christ’s transfiguration according to an early tradition of the church, the present Jebel <hi type="italic">et Tur</hi>, is a large truncated cone of limestone, which is almost perfectly insulated, and rises to the height of about a thousand feet, on the north-eastern border of the plain of Jezreel. The sides of the mountain are covered with a forest of oaks and wild pistachios, and upon its flat summit, which is about half an hour in circumference, there are the remains of ancient fortifications (see <hi type="italic">Robinson</hi>, Pal. iii. pp. 211ff., and <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, Pal. pp. 37, 38). The words “and take with thee 10,000 men” are not to be understood as signifying that Barak was to summon the people together upon the top of Mount Tabor, but the assembling of the people is presupposed; and all that is commanded is, that he was to proceed to Mount Tabor with the assembled army, and make his attack upon the enemy, who were encamped in the valley of Kishon, <hi type="italic">from that point.</hi> According to Jdg 4:10, the army was collected at Kedesh in Naphtali. <hi type="italic">Nachal Kishon</hi> is not only the brook <hi type="italic">Kishon</hi>, which is formed by streams that take their rise from springs upon Tabor and the mountains of Gilboa, flows in a north-westerly direction through the plain of Jezreel to the Mediterranean, and empties itself into the bay of Acca, and which is called <hi type="italic">Mukatta</hi> by the natives (see <hi type="italic">Rob</hi>. iii. pp. 472ff., and <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, pp. 39, 50), but the valley on both sides of the brook, i.e., the plain of Jezreel (see at <reference osisRef="Josh.17.16">Jos 17:16</reference>), where the greatest battles have been fought for the possession of Palestine from time immemorial down to the most recent times (see <hi type="italic">v. Raumer</hi>, pp. 40ff.).
entries.b2682aac3c1a0e8beaf87b87c71ef7d5c4c9eb80: Jdg 4:8-11 <div eID="gen3129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3130" type="x-p"/> Barak replied that he would not go unless she would go with him - certainly not for the reason suggested by <hi type="italic">Bertheau</hi>, viz., that he distrusted the divine promise given to him by Deborah, but because his mistrust of his own strength was such that he felt too weak to carry out the command of God. He wanted divine enthusiasm for the conflict, and this the presence of the prophetess was to infuse into both Barak and the army that was to be gathered round him. Deborah promised to accompany him, but announced to him as the punishment for this want of confidence in the success of his undertaking, that the prize of victory - namely, the defeat of the hostile general - should be taken out of his hand; for Jehovah would sell (i.e., deliver up) Sisera into the hand of a woman, viz., according to Jdg 4:17., into the hand of Jael.
